bib.title: Improving language models by retrieving from trillions of tokens

read.skipped: Qualitative colour-coded sample tables (Tables 6,7,16-21) and the per-subset figure grids (Figs 10-12) come out jumbled; read captions and surrounding text only. References skimmed for lineage.

question: Can a language model be improved by conditioning on chunks retrieved from a database of trillions of tokens, as an alternative to scaling parameters?
hypothesis: Retrieval from a massive database is a complementary path to scaling that decouples memorisation from model size and compute.
contributions: Retro, a retrieval-enhanced autoregressive LM with chunked cross-attention (linear in retrieved data) and a frozen BERT retriever
Scaling with model size (150M to 7B) and database size/number of neighbours; SOTA on Wikitext103 and Pile among large-data models; fine-tunes to QA
An evaluation methodology aware of train/test overlap (filtered bpb)

method.summary: Input of 2048 tokens is split into 64-token chunks; for each chunk the 2 nearest chunks (plus their continuations) are fetched by L2 distance on frozen BERT embeddings from a MassiveText database and encoded by a small bidirectional encoder; decoder layers every 3rd from layer 6 cross-attend to the previous chunk's neighbours via chunked cross-attention. Models are trained from scratch with a retrieval database of 600B tokens, or retro-fitted by freezing a pre-trained model and training only cross-attention and encoder.
method.task: retrieval-enhanced next-token pretraining and language modelling evaluation

datasets.name: MassiveText (multilingual version)
datasets.split: sampling weights: Web 55%, Books 25%, News 10%, Wikipedia 5%, GitHub 5%
datasets.preprocessing: SentencePiece, vocab 128,000; training docs with 13-gram MinHash Jaccard similarity >= 0.8 to any validation/test doc removed; Wikitext103 val/test articles removed from Wikipedia

datasets.name: Retrieval database (training)
datasets.split: same subsets as training data in proportion to sampling frequency
datasets.preprocessing: neighbours from the same document as the training sequence filtered out

datasets.name: Retrieval database (evaluation)
datasets.split: full union of MassiveText with Books sub-sampled to 4%

datasets.name: C4, Wikitext103, Curation Corpus, Lambada, The Pile, Wikipedia Sept 2021
datasets.size: Wikipedia Sept 2021: 23 articles; others not stated
datasets.split: C4 validation; Wikitext103 valid/test; Pile test (Enron Emails and YouTube Subtitles excluded)
datasets.preprocessing: Wikipedia Sept 2021 filtered for templated overlap; evaluated at sequence length 2048 with stride 1024

datasets.name: Natural Questions (FiD version with DPR passages)
datasets.preprocessing: format 'question: {question} \n answer: {answer}', left padded so 'answer:' ends the first 64-token chunk; each neighbour 'title: {title}, source: {source}'

models.name: Retro
models.architecture: decoder with chunked cross-attention plus 2-layer bidirectional neighbour encoder (d'=896, ~19M params)
models.context: 2048 tokens (n=2048, chunk m=64, k neighbours of r=128 tokens: 64 neighbour + 64 continuation)

other.retrieval: frozen BERT, L2 distance, SCaNN approximate kNN

models.name: Baseline transformer
models.architecture: Radford 2019 GPT-2-like, RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm, relative position encodings (Dai 2019)

models.name: Frozen BERT
models.architecture: BERT embedding of neighbour chunk N averaged over time as key

models.name: Jurassic-1, Gopher, GPT-3
models.params: 178B (Jurassic-1) / 280B (Gopher); GPT-3 size not stated in text

other.note: numbers copied from Lieber 2021 and Rae 2021

training.objective: retrieval-enhanced autoregressive log-likelihood (Eq 1); first chunk has no retrieval
training.lr_schedule: cosine decay with cycle length equal to total training tokens
training.warmup: linear from 1e-7 to max over first 750 steps
training.regularisation: ZeRO optimiser state sharding (infrastructure, not regularisation)

other.retro_fit_lr: 2e-4 -> 2e-5 (172M, 425M, 1.5B), 1e-4 -> 1e-5 (7.5B), batch 256, new weights only, cross-attn every 3rd layer from 6, 6M sequences (3% of pre-training)
other.wikitext103_baseline: 18 layers (Table 11; Sec 4.1 text says 24), d 1024, d_ffw 4096, 16 heads, seq len 3072, batch 128, Adam b1 0.9 b2 0.95 eps 1e-8, dropout 0.25, lr 1e-7 -> 2.5e-4 over 4,000 warmup steps, cosine to 2e-5 at 100,000 steps; checkpoint at step 35,000 used (valid ppl 21.58 at 75% overlap, 21.53 at 87.5%); Retro-fit from it, 2 neighbours trained, Wikipedia retrieval; training Retro from scratch overfit
other.nq_finetune: all weights of 7.5B Retro, 25,000 steps, batch 128, lr cosine 1e-6 -> 1e-7, 750-step linear ramp, dropout in decoder only, top 20 DPR neighbours at train and eval

inference.decoding: Lambada: greedy generation on the last word; other evaluation by likelihood
inference.samples: single run per model; no seeds or confidence intervals reported
inference.prompting: Curation Corpus: article + 'TL;DR:' + summary, bpb on summary only; NQ format given in datasets
inference.retrieval: SCaNN approx kNN on frozen BERT chunk embeddings, L2; 2 neighbours trained; evaluation default 2 (Fig 1 sweeps 1-100; 10 for Wikitext103); 10 ms per query on 2T tokens; retrieval re-done at the end of each generated chunk

metrics.name: bits-per-byte
metrics.definition: model log-likelihood per byte of text; tokenizer agnostic

metrics.name: filtered bpb(alpha)
metrics.definition: bpb over evaluation chunks whose longest common token substring with their 10 nearest training neighbours is at most alpha*64 tokens (Eq 5)

eval.protocol: Single trained model per configuration, no seeds, no significance tests reported.

availability.code: A simplified JAX Cca implementation is printed in Listing 1; no release stated
availability.data: MassiveText is DeepMind-internal (Rae et al. 2021); evaluation sets public

evidence.quote: In all cases, we train for 419,430,400,000 training tokens.

results.claim: A 7.5B Retro with a 2T-token database is comparable to GPT-3 and Jurassic-1 on the Pile with 25x fewer parameters.
results.setup: Pile test subsets (Enron Emails and YouTube Subtitles excluded), bits-per-byte, Retro 7.5B vs Jurassic-1 178B and Gopher 280B; their numbers copied from their papers; Retro beats them on a majority of subsets, not all.
results.quote: obtains comparable performance to GPT-3 and Jurassic-1 on the Pile, despite using 25× fewer parameters

results.claim: Retro 7.5B outperforms Jurassic-1 and Gopher on a majority of Pile test sets; it does not beat the 7B baseline on dm_mathematics and ubuntu_irc.
results.setup: Pile, 7.5B Retro vs 178B Jurassic-1 and 280B Gopher, relative bpb improvement over the 7B baseline.
results.quote: Overall, Retro 7.5B outperforms Jurassic-1 and Gopher on a majority of the test sets.

results.claim: Retro gain is constant across model sizes and comparable to multiplying parameters by about 10x (stated for C4; 'certain datasets' in the conclusion).
results.setup: C4 validation, bpb, 172M to 7.5B non-embedding params, training database 600B tokens, evaluation database 1.75T tokens.
results.quote: The performance gain of our retrieval models remains constant with model scale (left), and is comparable to multiplying the parameteric model size by ∼10×.

results.claim: C4 bpb with retrieval vs baseline at 7.5B.
results.setup: C4 eval, Table 14, 7.5B model, Retro[On] vs baseline.
results.table: Table 14, row C4 Eval bpb, 7.5B columns: baseline 0.78, Retro[On] 0.66

results.claim: Retro[Off] (retrieval disabled at evaluation) matches the baseline on C4 at every size.
results.table: Table 14, row C4 Eval bpb, Retro[Off] 7.5B column

results.claim: Growing the evaluation retrieval database improves C4 bpb for the 7.5B model.
results.setup: C4 eval, 7.5B Retro, varying evaluation database size; Table 14 rows C4 Eval bpb (2B) to (900B).
results.table: Table 14, row C4 Eval bpb (2B) 7.5B column 0.78; row C4 Eval bpb (900B) 7.5B column 0.71; full 0.66

results.claim: Despite training with 2 neighbours, more neighbours help at evaluation; the 172M model improves up to 10 neighbours and the 7B model up to 40, after which quality degrades.
results.quote: the 172M model improves with up to 10 neighbours, whereas the 7B model improves with up to 40 neighbours

results.claim: Wikitext103 test perplexity with full MassiveText retrieval is 3.92, which the authors say is partly leakage.
results.setup: Retro fine-tuned (Retro-fit) from an 18-layer Wikitext103 baseline, 10 neighbours at evaluation; baseline 22.96, Retro retrieving Wikipedia 18.97, kNN-LM (ours) 19.54.
results.note: Section 4.1 says the baseline has 24 layers; Table 11 lists 18 layers.
results.quote: The perplexities for retrieving from full MassiveText are quite low, which is partly due to partial overlap with Wikitext103 not caught by our deduplication.

results.claim: Retro-fitting needs only 6 million sequences (3% of pre-training sequences) and trains under 10% of weights at 7B.
results.setup: Frozen pre-trained decoder, new chunked cross-attention and neighbour encoder trained on MassiveText.
results.quote: requiring only 6 million sequences (3% of the pre-training sequences that we used)

results.claim: Fine-tuned Retro 7.5B reaches 45.5 exact match on Natural Questions, below FiD (51.4) and Emdr2 (52.5); closed-book 7B baseline is 30.4.
results.setup: NQ test exact match; all weights of 7.5B Retro fine-tuned 25,000 steps with top-20 DPR passages.
results.table: Table 5, row Retro 7.5B (DPR retrieval), column Test Accuracy

results.claim: Retro exploits train/eval leakage more strongly than baselines, but still beats them on chunks with under 8 shared contiguous tokens.
results.setup: Filtered bpb (Eq 5) on C4, Wikitext103, Curation Corpus, Wikipedia Sept 2021; alpha = 12.5%.
results.quote: Retro outperforms baseline models at all leakage levels, down to α = 12.5%.

results.claim: Only a modest fraction of Retro's gain is due to test set leakage.
results.setup: Authors' conclusion from the filtered evaluation.
results.quote: only a modest fraction of the gains obtained by Retro are due to test set leakage

results.claim: Ablation: attending to neighbours only gives 22% of the retrieval gain, continuations only 56%; using both is best.
results.setup: 247M model, 157B-token schedule, C4 eval bpb: Retro 0.822, neighbours N 0.950, continuations F 0.895, no retrieval 0.987.
results.quote: attending to neighbours only provides 22% of the performance

results.claim: Ablation: training with 1 neighbour is much worse (0.858) and 4 neighbours (0.847) gives no large gain over 2 (0.822) but costs more.
results.table: Table 13, rows 1 training neighbours 0.858, 4 training neighbours 0.847, Retro 0.822

results.claim: Retrieval at the chunk level makes the index tractable: kNN-LM needs 15 TB for 4B Wikipedia tokens; Retro needs 215 GB for Wikipedia and 93 TB for MassiveText.
results.quote: Retro only requires 215Gb to index our Wikipedia dataset, and 93Tb

results.claim: Retro nearest-neighbour lookup in a 2T-token database takes about 10 ms.
results.setup: SCaNN approximate search, amortised over a 64-token chunk.
results.quote: we can query our 2 trillion token database in 10 ms
retrieval reduces hallucinations (in line with the ﬁndings of Shuster et al. (2021))

limits: No seeds or confidence intervals; one model per configuration.
Training and evaluation data are the same corpus, so leakage cannot be removed; dedup missed Wikitext103 overlap (3.92 ppl).
Pile comparison excludes two subsets and uses other labs' published numbers; GPT-3 omitted from Fig 4.
On NQ, Retro under-performs FiD; authors hypothesise Retro relies less on encoder output; more than 20 neighbours does not help.
Retro does not beat the baseline on dm_mathematics and ubuntu_irc.
Claims that database updates keep the model current or remove data are argued (Sec 3.2), not measured.
Compute, hardware and wall-clock are not stated in the paper.
Possible bias and toxicity effects of retrieval flagged as needing further work.
